##### **Base metals: Economic concerns put prices under pressure** 

On a monthly average basis, base metal cash prices, with the exception of copper peaked in February.  For copper, the cash quote has been supported by the widening of the backwardation, which at one stage flared out to over $150/ tonne.  Copper nevertheless registered a month-on-month decline in April in terms of monthly average prices as three-month prices eased and eventu

ally the backwardation narrowed.  For most metals, we have noted a narrowing of trading ranges, particularly for those metals in over supply. The other feature is that price movements have generally reflected our view of the underlying fundamentals, with aluminium and nickel retreating significantly from the highs seen earlier this year.  The decline in lead and zinc has been more gradual despite the increase to reported stocks. 

Thomson Reuters GFMS has assessed all the latest market data and has revised its historical balances and extended our quarterly supply-demand balances out to the end of the second quarter of 2013.  For most metals, we have scaled back our forecasts for the remainder of this year. This reflects the variety of economic concerns, which have broadened since we last analysed our market balance and price projections.  Initially, the focus was on the deteriorating prospects for the Eurozone.  More recently, concerns have been voiced about the sustainability of the strong economic growth rates within China.  Although some of these worries have retreated, the data relating to specific end use industries, which are large consumers of base metals, remains bearish. 

The automobile industry highlights this trend.  Vehicle production last year was flat.  The weakness has been carried over to this year with Chinese auto sales in Q1, down 3.4% year-on-year at 4.79 million units, and output 1.8% lower at 4.78 million units.  The production of electrical generation equipment, washing machines and airconditioning units all registered declines in this period. 

The relatively lacklustre activity levels in some key consuming industries come against a background of rising inventories within China, particularly those held outside of Shanghai Futures Exchange warehouses.  Some of this stockpile represents material that is used as collateral for loans, however anecdotal evidence that we receive suggests that physical metal is increasingly available within China. So far, this has been slow to be reflected in reported trade flows.  We note, however, that the initial estimate of refined metal and copper product imports in April was the lowest level since August last year.  We believe that the Chinese trade data, particularly for copper, will show further declines as the second quarter data is fully rolled out.  Also we expect that the data on Europe will be relatively negative in this period, particularly as the political climate within the region is changing following recent elections in France, Greece and the Netherlands. 

In terms of production we do not expect any supply response.  From a cost point of view, it is the aluminium and nickel producers that are under the most pressure.  However, for aluminium there have been no further announcements of production cutbacks, and capacity (and output) continues to be raised in China.  For nickel, we are not aware of any cuts at the nickel pig iron sector, where the growing importance of the EAF rat

her than blast furnace producers is reducing the marginal cost of production. Still high prices for lead and zinc, together with elevated by-product prices makes production cuts unlikely. ILZSG has recently released its projections for mine and refined output this year which point to further gains in supply. This is in line with our forecasts, which are detailed in the lead and zinc sections. Our view on the supply side for copper and tin is essentially unchanged, with the producers still struggling to overcome the structural shortfall of mine capacity. The OECD Leading Economic indicator continued to inch higher in February, up to 100.5 from 100.3. This suggests that growth will pick up in the second half of the year with the United States and Japan putting in strong performances with the euroarea lagging. However, some of the more country specific indicators suggest that base metal demand conditions will remain lacklustre during the remainder of the second quarter. US consumer confidence, as measured by the University of Michigan, increased slightly in April to 76.4. This strong performance helped US automotive sales, which recorded a seasonally adjusted annualised rate of 14.4 million units in April. This was in line with the March pace, but down slightly from the 14.6 million level reported for the whole of the first quarter. The ISM purchasing managers’ index rose to 54.8 in April, up from 53.4 in March and the

to weaker employment numbers; however, we believe that improving consumer and business confidence will support economic activity and base metal demand in 2012. Eurozone industrial production rose 0.5% month-onmonth in February after a flat January. This unexpected improvement was still down 1.8% year-on-year however. More importantly, the PMIs for most of the leading Eurozone economies are still below 50%. The figure for the Eurozone as a whole fell for the third month in a row in April and at 45.9 is now back at the lows recorded in late 2011. Our favoured broad-based measure for the Japanese economy is the Tankan Survey. Sentiment among Japanese manufacturers failed to improve in the first quarter. The headline diffusion index of current conditions for large manufacturers remained unchanged at -4 points in the first quarter. This negative outcome is despite an easing in the value of the yen, aggressive monetary easing, and a brightening the profits and sales outlook in early 2012. This suggests that the manufacturing sector does not expect these encouraging signs to be maintained. Chinese industrial production grew 11.9% year-on-year in March – slightly above the combined January/February number of 11.4%. It indicates that the economy remains on a slower track, but is settling for a soft landing as of now. Of more concern was the fixed asset investment number, which fell to 20.9% over the first quarter compared to 21.5% over the first two months of the year. Slowing property is the primary reason. As we discuss in some of the individual sections, the performance of a number of key base metal consuming sectors have been particularly poor with weakness seen in the automotive, construction and air-conditioning sectors having been carried over to the first quarter of this year. Indian industrial production grew 4.1% year-on-year in February – while January’s 6.5% year-on-year growth was revised down to just 1.1%. This suggests that the Indian economy was in real trouble in the first quarter, particularly as the biggest slowdown was in capital machinery and related goods – heavy metal consuming sectors. The LME cash aluminium price was trading around $1,990/tonne at the time of writing, similar to the end-2011 price level. Whilst this environment remains, it seems likely that the capped-price/ elevated-premium situation will remain in place. ###### **Record premium levels flatter underlying demand conditions** 

Despite the pressures on outright prices, physical premiums have continued to ratchet higher as metal availability on the ground remains tight.  The large volume of cancelled metal warrants at the locations with the largest concentrations of metal, as noted above, are promoting huge delays for any buyers of “last resort” from LME inventories.  European dutyunpaid good western material is currently quoted around $145-155/tonne, compared to $140-150/tonne just a few days back, whilst duty-paid is about $210-220/tonne, some $10 more than reported in last month’s One Year Forecast. Despite this, the broader demand picture in Europe remains lacklustre, as highlighted below. 

US demand was estimated by the WBMS to be 4.3% lower for the year compared to 2010.  This figure does, though, appear to be lower than anecdotal reports (especially towards the end of the year) suggested.  Data for the first two months of 2012 indicate much healthier year-on-year growth.  A slew of recent corporate reports have pointed to some positive areas for demand.  Novelis has highlighted the US automotive market as a particular area of growth; this was underscored by April US auto sales data, which showed a rise to an annualised rate of 14.4 million units.   Alcoa raised its demand growth for the aerospace sector from 10 to 13-14%, with global growth in 2012 expected to realise 7% (Thomson Reuters GFMS forecasts 5.3%).  Indeed, Alcoa recently raised prices for some aerospace plate products by 5%, due to higher materials costs and increased demand. Hydro reported improved demand for extruded aluminium products in North American transport and automotive markets, whilst Kaiser and Noranda also noted the strength of the auto and aerospace sectors; the latter being driven by “increasing build rates, larger airframes and monolithic design.”  The Aluminum Association said that North American demand (domestic shipments plus imports) for aluminium products rose 8% in February year-on-year and 1.7% month-on-month.  Its index of Net New Orders of aluminium mill products rose 4% month-on-month in March, but was down 3.4% year-on-year. 

Although US demand looks slightly better, most consumers seem to think that spiking premiums are unwarranted; more a reflection of the ongoing LME contango and cash-and-carry deals.  The US Midwest premium has recently been quoted at $209-215/tonne; but there have been indications of $220/ tonne (10¢/lb) or higher, levels not seen before.  Japanese spot premiums have also surged higher, being reported at $150/tonne and even

as high as $165-180/tonne. The WBMS estimated that total European consumption increased by 2.5% in 2011, but there was a notable monthon-month decline in December. Data for January and February 2012 indicate a sharp year-on-year fall. Of the major consumers within the area, German, Italy France and Belgium are down year-on-year, whilst Russia and Spain are estimated to be flat. ###### **Market outlook** 

As discussed above, we have our revised our supply demand balance projections.  Our overall view of a market in oversupply is unchanged and, in fact, we have increased our forecast of the surplus for this year to 352,000 tonnes from our previous forecast of 218,000 tonnes.  Importantly, we also expect the market to remain in surplus in the first half of 2013 (+154,000 tonnes).   In terms of prices, we have scaled back our projections; however we have not forecast a collapse in prices despite the oversupply, as we expect that more buoyant conditions elsewhere in the sector will provide some support. 

Our high case ( **Scenario B** ) is predicated on a stronger demand environment, which realistically is unlikely to emerge until the latter part of this year.  The other factor is that Chinese refined production growth is limited leading to a further increase to imports, which rose by 50.2% to 131,000 tonnes in the first quarter.  Also despite the stock overhang there is the question of the availability of this material which could provide price support; however as in the aluminium market this might be more reflected by higher physical premiums.  Under our high case, we project an average annual price of $2,170/tonne in 2012 with the prospects of further gains in 2013 as the impact of mine closures becomes more of an issue. 

Under the low case ( **Scenario C** ), the price inelastic nature of zinc supply will come to the fore.  If demand conditions fail to pick up, prices will spend the bulk of the next twelve months below $2,000/tonne.  It should be noted that our low case forecast of $1,895/tonne for this year is above the 2009 low of $1,648/tonne, so this alternative forecast can be considered fairly conservative.
